readings.contests: Comparison with DNA pressed other units to trade subjective judgment for the objectivity DNA profiling was taken to embody.
readings.alternative: The comparison concerns making expert work inspectable afterward, redistributing who can question an analysis, while judgment remains inside DNA work too.

readings.contests: Narcotics analysts kept crystal testing because instrumentation offended their values of autonomy and variety, and their professional-debate pathway imposed no immediate need to change.
readings.alternative: The unit kept crystal tests because statutory turnaround and only two instruments left no other way to clear its caseload; compliance was anticipated and priced.

readings.contests: DNA profiling stood as the objective gold standard, a fixed benchmark against which the other units' techniques and values were measured as compatible or incompatible.
readings.alternative: The DNA unit is one more case: its work is judgment negotiated with reviewers, and its occupation was itself challenged and evaluated earlier.

readings.contests: Toxicology embraced change while firearms and narcotics resisted it, a contrast the paper explains through each group's values and technique.
readings.alternative: All units accepted changes adding to the record and refused changes replacing personal judgment; the contrast reflects which kind of change each was offered.

readings.contests: All three units fell within the comparison's reach, leaving only the outer boundary of neighboring occupations as an open question.
readings.alternative: The boundary may run between the three units, with toxicology outside the comparison's reach, so the comparison reached two units and changed neither.

readings.contests: Narcotics analysts resisted changing their local practices.
readings.alternative: The outcome is a snapshot of an unsettled situation when fieldwork ended: nothing was yet required, so holding on reflects no mandate and capacity limits.

readings.contests: Each unit's response was jointly shaped by institutional pathway, technique and occupational values.
readings.alternative: Whether analysts expected a personal local court challenge alone decided change; values merely describe how units talked about outcomes exposure had already settled.

readings.contests: Narcotics analysts' worry arose from a professional debate over technique renewed by DNA comparison, and they resisted because instrumentation offended their values.
readings.alternative: The dispute is a power struggle over standard-setting, in which an Eastern coalition could use DNA's prestige to make its own equipment compulsory nationwide.

readings.contests: Each unit's values arise from the work it does and are learned through practicing its technique.
readings.alternative: Unit values partly result from self-sorting: analysts who disliked repetitive instrument work left toxicology for narcotics, so values reflect selected memberships.

readings.contests: Toxicology changed and firearms did not because toxicology's court challenge was local and immediate while firearms' was distant.
readings.alternative: The units differed in whether an accreditor-scheduled plan already answered the challenge; the court case's nearness set only the timing.

readings.contests: Each unit's values arise from the work it does and are learned through practicing its technique.
readings.alternative: The toxicology–narcotics contrast partly results from staffing and self-selection, as analysts disliking repetitive work moved units, producing distinct cultures.

readings.contests: Status and power mattered much less to the units' responses than the nature of their work and values.
readings.alternative: Responses were moves to protect each unit's standing and irreplaceability against a director treating analysts as interchangeable.

readings.contests: Narcotics resisted while toxicology adopted change because instrumentation offended narcotics values of variety, autonomy and craft judgment but fit toxicology's values.
readings.alternative: The units differed in how much routine work the change would displace and what instruments, time and caseload it would cost.

readings.contests: All three units encountered the same comparison with DNA profiling and answered it differently.
readings.alternative: Only firearms met a DNA comparison; toxicology and narcotics met demands for uncertainty or reviewable output that participants did not tie to DNA.

readings.contests: Toxicology changed and firearms did not because toxicology's court challenge was local and immediate while firearms' was distant.
readings.alternative: A standing accreditation requirement and existing plan made the difference; the immediate challenge accounted only for when toxicology's reports changed.

readings.contests: Narcotics resisted despite a compatible instrument technique because instrumentation offended their values of variety, autonomy and craft judgment.
readings.alternative: Resistance defended a workable production system under legal deadlines and limited equipment; narcotics faced replacing its main route, toxicology merely added calculations.

readings.contests: Comparison with DNA pressed other units to trade subjective judgment for the objectivity DNA profiling was taken to embody.
readings.alternative: The central change redistributes the ability to check expert conclusions through durable records, making control over later scrutiny the organizing issue.

readings.contests: Narcotics resisted despite a compatible instrument technique because instrumentation offended their values of variety, autonomy and craft judgment.
readings.alternative: Resistance defended a workable service: knowing GC/MS did not mean having capacity to run the whole caseload on it under turnaround constraints.

readings.contests: Firearms examiners rejected the evaluation and did not change their local practices.
readings.alternative: Firearms had already adopted the reviewable-record part of the DNA model, refusing only numbers; the embrace/resist column hides a shared documentary shift.

readings.contests: Each unit's values arise from the work it does and are learned through practicing its technique.
readings.alternative: Unit values partly record who came, stayed and left; narcotics' dislike of standardized work was brought from toxicology by those who transferred.

readings.contests: Firearms examiners rejected the evaluation and did not change their local practices.
readings.alternative: Firearms had already met the demand through a countersigned image record; it refused only statistics, so units differ in which DNA piece they took up.

readings.contests: Toxicology changed its reporting because DNA comparison reached it through an imminent local court challenge.
readings.alternative: The change was an existing accreditation reform whose content predated the pressure; litigation, with DNA as courtroom reference, only accelerated its timetable.

readings.contests: Toxicology changed its reporting because DNA comparison reached it through an imminent local court challenge.
readings.alternative: The change was a planned accreditation step brought forward by a DUI defense tactic; DNA enters only through the author's statements.

readings.contests: Toxicology changed its reporting because DNA comparison reached it through an imminent local court challenge.
readings.alternative: It was ordinary ISO-based standards compliance already under way, brought forward by a court date; the DNA link is the analyst's attachment.

readings.contests: Each unit's response was jointly shaped by institutional pathway, technique and occupational values.
readings.alternative: Units share one rule: revise when a credible local challenge makes continuing costly; values only supply the language and form of adjustment.

readings.contests: Occupational values and technique explain why firearms, toxicology and narcotics responded differently to the DNA comparison.
readings.alternative: All three responses track what change would cost in instruments, staff time and deadlines; values are merely the language expressing those costs.

readings.contests: Each unit's values arise from the work it does and are learned through practicing its technique.
readings.alternative: Values partly reflect sorting within one lab through placement, reassignment and transfer, describing who ended up at which bench.

readings.contests: Toxicology changed its reporting because DNA comparison reached it through an imminent local court challenge.
readings.alternative: The change completed an existing accreditation project ahead of schedule; a courtroom deadline set timing, and DNA may not have determined its content.

groups.point: The DNA comparison is about making expert work reviewable afterward, not about replacing subjectivity with objectivity.
Narcotics resistance reflects capacity and cost constraints (deadlines, few instruments, displaced routine) rather than values.
The DNA unit is not a fixed objective benchmark but one more judgment-laden unit with its own history of evaluation.
Units accepted additive record changes and refused judgment-replacing ones; the contrast reflects the kind of change offered.
The spillover's boundary runs between the three units, with toxicology outside the comparison's reach.
The narcotics outcome is a provisional snapshot of an unsettled situation, not resistance.
Expected local court exposure alone decides whether units change; values only describe the decision.
The narcotics dispute is a regional power struggle over control of standard-setting.
Unit values partly result from analysts sorting themselves among units, not only from the work.
A standing accreditation requirement, not immediacy of the court pathway, separated toxicology from firearms.
Responses were status moves protecting each unit's standing and irreplaceability.
Units faced different demands from different sources, not one DNA comparison.
Firearms had already adopted DNA-style reviewable documentation, refusing only statistics.
Toxicology's change was a prior accreditation project accelerated by litigation, not a DNA spillover.
All three responses follow the cost of change to each unit, with values as its language.
